correctness.rationale: At t≤1/2 the third functional is redundant; the two diagonal vertices of the square attain 2. Above the threshold put a=1/t−1 and r=|a|. The six vertices are the three signed pairs listed in the proof. Selecting two norming functionals for x+y and x−y gives 2C_NJ as the maximum squared norm of the corresponding operators on the unrestricted ℓ²-sum. The dual calculation tests pf_i±qf_j on the vertices; sign symmetry permits p,q≥0. For a≥0, (f₁,f₂) attains the envelope (p+q)²+max(p+rq,rp+q)². For a<0 the distinct pairs involving f₃ instead give one norm p+q and the other max(p,rp+q), up to symmetry; the latter attains the envelope when q≥p. The other pairs, including equal facets, cannot exceed it. By symmetry p≥q maximizes the Rayleigh form with rows (2,1+r) and (1+r,1+r²); its positive top eigenvector has p≥q by the diagonal ordering. This gives the stated radical and agrees with the explicit primal witnesses by applying the relevant two-facet operator. The profile has positive derivative in r, with endpoint derivatives 1/√5 and 1 at r=0 and 1. Substitution verifies all three expansions. For this finite-dimensional norm, equality in the universal bound 2 is precisely the equal-norm attained case where both sum and difference saturate the triangle bound, justifying the non-squareness conclusion.
residual_risks: The finite grid and random-vector test were not rerun. The exact finite-facet and Rayleigh calculations, not sampled parameters, cover the continuum. The scalar field is real.

evidence: The accessible RIMS formulas concern symmetric absolute functions or global comparison with the Euclidean function. Here ψ(z)=max(1−(1−c)z,z) is nonsymmetric and lies above √((1−z)²+z²) near 0 and below it near 1 for 0<c<1. The all-exponent Day–James result has a fixed hexagon, not a varying facet.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Changing exponent on a fixed ball cannot be substituted for moving a facet while keeping the quotient exponent two; the available symmetric/global absolute-norm hypotheses fail here.

evidence: Take s=(u+v)/2 and d=t(u−v), giving max(|d|,|s|+c|d|), c=1/(2t). This is exactly N_γ with γ=1−c in the Banach–Mazur record, not just a similar hexagon. Evaluating the dual on the vertices (±1,0),(±(1−c),±1) and swapping coordinates replaces c by 1−c, explaining the symmetry in |1−2c|.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The linear equivalence and duality must be accounted for when identifying constants previously determined. The known distance to Euclidean space in this family is a different invariant; an unrestricted NJ value is not recovered from that distance alone.

originality.rationale: The hexagon family is classical and the regular-hexagon value is already covered. The supported distinct claim is the unrestricted constant along the whole deformation, including the exact threshold and global minimum along that family. Available broader formulas and the prior exact same-family Banach–Mazur result do not settle that claim.
residual_risks: The Komuro–Saito–Mitani 2010 and Saito–Kato–Takahashi 2000 full texts were not available, and the Yang–Wang 2006 DOI did not yield its full text; endpoint coverage is independently present in the local generalized profile. An uninspected absolute-norm formula could affect priority.

Classical same-family Banach–Mazur profile and fixed-hexagon NJ comparator
value.rationale: The exact unrestricted NJ profile is a motivated comparison of non-squareness across a classical norm deformation. It records a sharp optimum, transition and explicit extremizers while separating the unrestricted invariant from equal-norm and isosceles variants; none of these continuum conclusions is obtained merely by recomputing the known endpoint.
residual_risks: Optimality is only within this real two-dimensional deformation, not among all hexagons or all normed planes.
